verses.text: Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished all his house.

For he built the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Its length was one hundred cubits,  its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits, on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars.
It was covered with cedar above over the forty-five beams, that were on the pillars, fifteen in a row.
There were beams in three rows, and window was facing window in three ranks.
All the doors and posts were made square with beams: and window was facing window in three ranks.
He made the porch of pillars. Its length was fifty cubits and its width thirty cubits; with a porch before them, and pillars and a threshold before them.
He made the porch of the throne where he was to judge, even the porch of judgment; and it was covered with cedar from floor to floor.
His house where he was to dwell, the other court within the porch, was of the like work. He made also a house for Pharaoh’s daughter (whom Solomon had taken as wife), like this porch.
All these were of costly stones, even of cut stone, according to measure, sawed with saws, inside and outside, even from the foundation to the coping, and so on the outside to the great court.
The foundation was of costly stones, even great stones, stones of ten cubits, and stones of eight cubits.
Above were costly stones, even cut stone, according to measure, and cedar wood.
The great court around had three courses of cut stone, and a course of cedar beams; like the inner court of Yahweh’s house and the porch of the house.
King Solomon sent and brought Hiram out of Tyre.

He was the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in brass; and he was filled with wisdom and understanding and skill, to work all works in brass. He came to king Solomon, and performed all his work.
For he fashioned the two pillars of brass, eighteen cubits high apiece; and a line of twelve cubits encircled either of them.
He made two capitals of molten brass, to set on the tops of the pillars. The height of the one capital was five cubits, and the height of the other capital was five cubits.
There were nets of checker work, and wreaths of chain work, for the capitals which were on the top of the pillars; seven for the one capital, and seven for the other capital.
So he made the pillars; and there were two rows around on the one network, to cover the capitals that were on the top of the pillars: and he did so for the other capital.
The capitals that were on the top of the pillars in the porch were of lily work, four cubits.
There were capitals above also on the two pillars, close by the belly which was beside the network. There were two hundred pomegranates in rows around the other capital.
He set up the pillars at the porch of the temple. He set up the right pillar, and called its name Jachin; and he set up the left pillar, and called its name Boaz.
On the top of the pillars was lily work: so the work of the pillars was finished.
He made the molten sea of ten cubits from brim to brim, round in shape. Its height was five cubits; and a line of thirty cubits encircled it.
Under its brim around there were buds which encircled it for ten cubits, encircling the sea. The buds were in two rows, cast when it was cast.

It stood on twelve oxen, three looking toward the north, and three looking toward the west, and three looking toward the south, and three looking toward the east; and the sea was set on them above, and all their hindquarters were inward.
It was a hand width thick. Its brim was worked like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held two thousand baths.
He made the ten bases of brass. The length of one base was four cubits, four cubits its width, and three cubits its height.
The work of the bases was like this: they had panels; and there were panels between the ledges;
and on the panels that were between the ledges were lions, oxen, and cherubim; and on the ledges there was a pedestal above; and beneath the lions and oxen were wreaths of hanging work.
Every base had four bronze wheels, and axles of brass; and the four feet of it had supports. The supports were cast beneath the basin, with wreaths at the side of each.

Its mouth within the capital and above was a cubit. Its mouth was round after the work of a pedestal, a cubit and a half; and also on its mouth were engravings, and their panels were square, not round.
The four wheels were underneath the panels; and the axles of the wheels were in the base. The height of a wheel was a cubit and half a cubit.
The work of the wheels was like the work of a chariot wheel. Their axles, and their rims, and their spokes, and their naves, were all of cast metal.
There were four supports at the four corners of each base. Its supports were of the base itself.
In the top of the base there was a round band half a cubit high; and on the top of the base its supports and its panels were of the same.
On the plates of its supports, and on its panels, he engraved cherubim, lions, and palm trees, each in its space, with wreaths all around.
He made the ten bases in this way: all of them had one casting, one measure, and one form.
He made ten basins of brass. One basin contained forty baths;  and every basin was four cubits; and on every one of the ten bases one basin.
He set the bases, five on the right side of the house, and five on the left side of the house. He set the sea on the right side of the house eastward and toward the south.
Hiram made the basins, the shovels, and the basins. So Hiram finished doing all the work that he worked for king Solomon in Yahweh’s house:
the two pillars; the two bowls of the capitals that were on the top of the pillars; the two networks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the top of the pillars;
the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks; two rows of pomegranates for each network, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars;
the ten bases; the ten basins on the bases;
the one sea; the twelve oxen under the sea;
the pots; the shovels; and the basins: even all these vessels, which Hiram made for king Solomon, in Yahweh’s house, were of burnished brass.
The king cast them in the plain of the Jordan, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan.
Solomon left all the vessels unweighed, because there were so many of them. The weight of the brass could not be determined.
Solomon made all the vessels that were in Yahweh’s house: the golden altar and the table that the show bread was on, of gold;
and the lamp stands, five on the right side, and five on the left, before the inner sanctuary, of pure gold; and the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of gold;

the cups, the snuffers, the basins, the spoons, and the fire pans, of pure gold; and the hinges, both for the doors of the inner house, the most holy place, and for the doors of the house, of the temple, of gold.

Thus all the work that king Solomon did in Yahweh’s house was finished. Solomon brought in the things which David his father had dedicated, the silver, the gold, and the vessels, and put them in the treasuries of Yahweh’s house.

footnotes.content: Thirteen years for Solomon's own house—longer than the temple's building time. How easily we spend more labor on what we see daily than on what belongs to the Lord. Yet even in this human preference, the work is called 'finished,' completed and sound.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The House of the Forest of Lebanon: cedar pillars in four rows held the beams. Cedar itself speaks—the wood that doesn't rot, that stood in temple and palace alike. It's a reminder that lasting things rest on strong foundations beneath us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Covered with cedar, overlaid with light—the beams held everything. There's something tender in noticing how the crafted parts work together, each one supporting the whole. The Lord works this way with us too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Window facing window, light meeting light from three sides. Someone understood that a building needs to breathe, to let the outside in. Even the grandest house is meant to live in, not merely admire.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Square doors and posts, square windows. Deliberate, orderly, made to last. The craftsmanship shows respect for the work and for those who will inhabit it—not rushed, not careless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A porch of pillars—the threshold where the outside world becomes inside. These structures frame a moment, a pause. They tell you: something matters here. Enter with awareness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The porch of judgment—where Solomon sits to judge. Built to last, cedar from floor to floor. The Lord calls rulers to decide justly, and here the very building material witnesses: permanence, truth-telling, weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A house for Pharaoh's daughter, like the porch. Solomon honors his wife's place—built of the same quality, the same care. Marriage, even foreign-made as this was, deserved the beauty of good work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Costly stones, cut and measured, sawed with care—inside and outside, from foundation to roof. The Lord sees what no one else will see; we honor Him by doing unseen things well.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Foundation stones of ten and eight cubits—massive, immovable, hidden. A building's true strength is what no one looks at. The same is true of a life lived well.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Costly stones above, cedar wood interspersed. Different materials working together—stone and wood, each with its own nature, both needed. The body of Christ works this way, different gifts, one purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three courses of cut stone, then cedar—a rhythm. The courtyard mirrors the temple's court. Beauty isn't invented new each time; it echoes what has proven true. The Lord repeats His mercies fresh each morning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon sent for Hiram from Tyre—a master craftsman. The king knew where skill lived and went to fetch it. We too must learn: pride won't build; only humility to ask, and gratitude for the gifted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hiram: widow's son, his father a Tyrian metalworker, filled with wisdom and skill. Here's a man whose gifts span generations—learned from a father, raised by a faithful mother. Skill and character grow in humble soil.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two brass pillars, eighteen cubits high—visible from far off. They announce something: 'Here stands the Lord's house.' We live so often small; sometimes we're called to speak large.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Molten brass capitals, five cubits each. The tops of the pillars crown them—beauty reaches highest. Even our strength deserves to be crowned with grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nets of checker work, chains of wreaths—decoration that holds. The ornament isn't mere display; it binds and strengthens. In life too, the beautiful things often do the binding work we can't see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two rows around to cover the capitals—symmetry, care, completeness. Nothing is left unfinished or exposed needlessly. The Lord finishes what He begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lily work on the capitals—flowers carved in brass. Even metal blooms here. The Lord loves to hide beauty in unexpected places; we find it when we look close.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two hundred pomegranates in rows—abundance made visible, made orderly. The fruit speaks of life and seed; the number speaks of generosity. The Lord delights in plenty offered honestly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jachin and Boaz—'He will establish' and 'In Him is strength.' The pillar names proclaim the Lord's character at the entrance to His house. Names matter; what we proclaim shapes what people remember.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Finished. The work of the pillars done, crowned with lily work. 'Finished' is a word the Lord loves—it speaks of completion, rest, satisfaction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The molten sea, ten cubits from brim to brim, held two thousand baths—the great basin for cleansing. Water speaks of life and purification; a sea of it says: abundance for washing, restoration always available.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Buds under the brim, cast as one with the sea. Life adorns even the unseen parts. The Lord doesn't save beauty only for what others see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve oxen beneath, three facing each direction—strength holds up cleansing. East, west, north, south: the whole world held in service. Labor and animal strength: humble, faithful, bearing the weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A hand-width thick, brim like a lily-flower—delicate and strong. The best vessels hold beauty and function in balance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten bases of brass, each four cubits by four, three high. Something must hold up the vessels; even in the temple, infrastructure matters. The unglamorous work upholds the sacred.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Panels between ledges—structure holding structure. The layering repeats: one thing supports another, all the way down. We stand on a chain of mercies we rarely trace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lions, oxen, cherubim on the panels—wild beasts and heavenly ones carved together. All creation serves the Lord's house. Nothing is beneath His notice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four wheels under each base, axles of brass, supports cast beneath—mobility built into steadiness. These bases move because they're needed; service is their design.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A round mouth like a pedestal, engraved and square—ornament and utility. Even the opening is shaped with intention. The Lord makes vessels fit for use.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wheels a cubit and a half high, four to each base. Precise, proportional. Even the humble wheel is measured carefully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wheels worked like chariot wheels—axles, rims, spokes, all of cast metal. Function copied from what works; wisdom borrows from experience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four supports at the corners—a base strong in all directions. Stability isn't an accident; it comes from support placed thoughtfully at every angle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Round band on top, supports and panels of one piece—unity in design. One thing flows from another. The Lord makes wholes, not fragments.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cherubim, lions, palm trees engraved—each in its space, with wreaths. The craftsman knew each element needed room. Crowding beauty spoils it; grace needs space.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All ten bases made one way—same casting, measure, form. Consistency speaks of mind and care. The Lord's work endures because it is faithful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten basins, forty baths each—twenty thousand baths of water capacity. So much to cleanse, so much need. The Lord provides more than barely enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five bases on the right, five on the left—balanced provision. East side, south side—the sea placed where light comes, where it catches the day. Water and light together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hiram finished all the work for the Lord's house. A man's work, complete and offered. This is the dignity we're made for: to finish well what we've been given to do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The pillars and their capitals—the two bowls on top. The list that follows is his work: bronze vessels, each one counted, each one known. The Lord misses nothing we make.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four hundred pomegranates—two rows for each network. Multiply them and you see abundance: even the ornaments are abundant. When we give to the Lord, we give generously.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten bases, ten basins—matched pairs, multiple copies. Repetition of the good thing. The Lord loves to multiply mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One sea, twelve oxen. The great vessel and its strength. Numbers that circle back to the tribes, to completion, to the whole people held.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pots, shovels, basins—every vessel burnished brass. Even the everyday tools are beautiful, polished. The Lord teaches us that common work deserves dignity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cast in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan—the Jordan plain. The Lord's house is built with materials from His land, worked in the dust. We are earth serving Heaven.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: So many vessels that the weight couldn't be determined—abundance beyond counting. Solomon's generosity mirrors the Lord's. When we give to Him, we can't outgive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Golden altar and table of shewbread—gold within, sacred vessels. Invisible to most, but where the Lord is worshipped, all is precious.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five lamp stands on the right, five on the left—light given symmetrically. The Lord illuminates completely, not partially. His light reaches every corner.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cups, snuffers, basins, spoons, fire pans—all of pure gold. Down to the smallest tool, the smallest object. The Lord values completeness and purity in all things.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the work finished, the vessels treasured and placed—the temple complete. Readers today hear an echo: when we offer our work to the Lord, it becomes treasure, held safe in His house. As of 2026-10, that promise still holds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
